title: Postpartum Psychosis: Emergency Assessment and Mother and Baby Unit Admission

evidenceAudit.scope: Recognition of postpartum psychosis, immediate specialist assessment, mother and baby unit admission and medicine safety around breastfeeding, from NICE CG192.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The last 14,035 characters of the CG192 text were not read.
No Saudi guideline on perinatal psychosis was opened; availability of mother and baby units in Saudi Arabia was not verified.
CG192 gives no doses; drug choice is for the perinatal psychiatrist.
Recommendations 1.8.22–1.8.23 (ECT, rapid tranquillisation) appear under pregnancy and are not applied to the postnatal period here.
EPDS, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 cut-off scores are not given in CG192.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1 to 2 in 1,000 women who have given birth and can become very severe extremely quickly. It is often accompanied by manic or depressive symptoms. Women with bipolar I disorder are at particular risk, but it can occur with no psychiatric history. Bipolar disorder shows a higher relapse rate and first presentation in the postnatal period, mostly in the first few weeks. Past or present severe mental illness, or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness, raises risk in the first 2 weeks.

symptoms: Sudden onset of manic, psychotic or severe depressive symptoms in the first weeks after childbirth.
physicalSigns: Rapid worsening of mental state over hours to days.
Mania or depressive features recorded at assessment.
redFlags: Sudden-onset symptoms in the first 2 weeks after childbirth, especially with past or present severe mental illness or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness.
Need for inpatient mental health care within 12 months of childbirth: mother and baby unit admission is the norm.
Taking lithium, valproate or carbamazepine, or clozapine while breastfeeding.
precipitants: Previous severe mental illness or severe perinatal illness in a first-degree relative.
Stopping lithium in pregnancy, which raises relapse risk.

differentials.condition: Relapse of bipolar disorder after childbirth
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Known bipolar disorder, especially after stopping lithium; same emergency pathway.
Monitored with validated tools (EPDS, PHQ-9, GAD-7); psychosis or mania needs urgent specialist assessment.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and refer
actions: Be alert in the first 2 weeks after childbirth, particularly with past or present severe mental illness or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness.
For sudden-onset symptoms, refer to a secondary mental health service, preferably specialist perinatal, for immediate assessment within 4 hours of referral.

clinicalManagement.title: Admit to a mother and baby unit
actions: A woman needing inpatient mental health care within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit unless there are specific reasons not to.
Units usually have 6 to 12 beds and work closely with community services.

clinicalManagement.title: Choose medicines with a perinatal psychiatrist
actions: Review, adjust, start or restart psychotropic medicines once medically stable.
Encourage breastfeeding unless taking carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium; support her choice of feeding method.
Do not offer valproate to women planning pregnancy, pregnant or considering breastfeeding.
Do not offer depot antipsychotics to women considering breastfeeding unless she responds well to a depot and has a history of non-adherence to oral medicine.

clinicalManagement.title: Protect the infant
actions: Monitor the baby for adverse effects of maternal psychotropic medicine during breastfeeding.
Carry out a full neonatal assessment after exposure in pregnancy.
Lithium may reach toxic levels in breast milk: monitor levels more frequently.

medicationPlan.note: CG192 sets no doses. Antipsychotic and lithium choice and dosing are decided by the perinatal psychiatrist with breastfeeding, infant monitoring and lithium level checks. Valproate must not be offered in pregnancy planning, pregnancy or breastfeeding. SFDA registration was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Within 4 hours of referral for sudden-onset symptoms (Rec 1.5.12).
First 2 weeks after childbirth with past or present severe mental illness or family history (Rec 1.5.11).
Specialist mother and baby unit within 12 months of childbirth unless specific reasons not to (Rec 1.10.1).

teaching.scope: Recognition of postpartum psychosis, immediate specialist assessment, mother and baby unit admission and medicine safety around breastfeeding, from NICE CG192.
learningObjectives: Recognise postpartum psychosis risk and presentation.
Arrange specialist assessment within 4 hours and mother and baby unit admission.
pitfalls: Treating sudden-onset symptoms as routine postnatal low mood.
Separating mother and baby by default when a mother and baby unit is available.
Missing lithium accumulation in breast milk.
keyPoints: Immediate assessment within 4 hours of referral.
Admit to a mother and baby unit within 12 months of childbirth.
Valproate is not offered to women who may breastfeed or conceive.

patientEducation: Explain to the woman and family that postpartum psychosis is a medical emergency that responds to treatment.
Explain infant monitoring if breastfeeding on medicine.
lifestyleAndDiet: Protect sleep and a safe, supervised environment with the baby.
mdtReferrals: Specialist perinatal mental health team; mother and baby unit; obstetrics; neonatology or paediatrics; health visitor or primary care.
dischargeCriteria: Stable mental state agreed by the perinatal team.
Medication plan, feeding plan and relapse-warning plan agreed with the woman and family.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Regular monitoring of symptoms through pregnancy and the postnatal period, especially the first few weeks after childbirth; review of psychotropic medicine and infant monitoring by the perinatal team.
